stem: The PV of the CCA tax shield (PVCCA) is:
options: the present value of the CCA deductions claimed, before any tax effect
the tax payable on any recapture when the asset is sold
the present value of all future CCA × T_C, valued as a perpetuity growing at −d
the salvage value of the asset discounted back N years to today
explanation: The shields CCA_t × T_C shrink at the rate d, so the stream is a growing perpetuity with g = −d. PVCCA is the present value of the tax saved, not of the CCA itself.

stem: Which expression is the base PVCCA (no first-year adjustment and no sale)?
options: I0 × d × T_C/(k − d)
I0 × T_C/(k + d)
I0 × d × T_C/(k + d)
explanation: Gordon growth with CCA_1 × T_C = I0 d T_C as the first flow and g = −d gives I0 d T_C/(k + d). Using k − d treats the shield as growing; omitting d drops the first-year CCA; (1 − T_C) confuses a shield with an after-tax expense.

stem: Which first-year factor goes into PVCCA for a new asset under the Accelerated Investment Incentive?
explanation: AII front-loads the claim: 1.5 of the perpetuity starting now less 0.5 of it starting a year later gives 1.5 − 0.5/(1 + k) = (1.5k + 1)/(1 + k).

stem: In PVCCA, the term [S_N × d × T_C/(k + d)] × 1/(1 + k)^N represents:
options: the tax on the capital gain when the asset is sold
the shield lost because CCA stops after the sale in year N
the after-tax proceeds of the sale in year N
the CCA tax shield actually received in year N
explanation: After the sale, CCA is no longer claimed on the asset's S_N. The PV at year N of that lost stream is S_N d T_C/(k + d); discounting it N years gives its value today.

stem: How does PVCCA differ for an asset sold in year N versus an asset that is never sold within the horizon (the pool stays open)?
options: Sold: add the lost-tail term; not sold: subtract the lost-tail term
Sold: replace k with N in the denominator; not sold: leave k unchanged
Sold: subtract the lost tail S_N d T_C/(k + d)/(1 + k)^N; not sold: no subtraction
There is no difference; the lost-tail term is always included
explanation: When the asset is sold, CCA on it stops, so that stream is removed. If nothing is sold, CCA continues forever and the base formula applies.

stem: Which of the following is NOT an input to the PVCCA formula?
options: The sale price S_N
The CCA rate d
The corporate tax rate T_C
The asset's UCC at the date of sale
explanation: The salvage term uses the sale price S_N, not the UCC. UCC at sale matters for recapture and terminal loss, not for PVCCA.

stem: Why is the denominator in PVCCA (k + d) rather than (k − d)?
options: The shield declines at rate d, so it is a growing perpetuity with g = −d and k − (−d) = k + d
Because tax is paid at the end of each year, which adds d to the rate
Because the half-year rule shifts the discount rate up by d
Because d is added to k to reflect the added risk of the asset
explanation: Gordon growth gives PV = first flow/(k − g). The CCA shield shrinks, so g = −d, and the denominator becomes k + d.

stem: Why is the salvage term in PVCCA multiplied by 1/(1 + k)^N?
options: The salvage proceeds arrive at year N and are taxed then
The lost shields begin after year N; their value at year N is discounted to today
The asset's UCC is reduced by a factor of (1 + k) each year after the sale
It adjusts the first-year factor for the half-year rule and AII regime
explanation: S_N d T_C/(k + d) is a value at year N (a perpetuity valued one period before its first payment). Dividing by (1 + k)^N converts it to today's dollars.

stem: With k = 10%, the CCA rate doubles from 10% to 20% (all else equal). What happens to the base PVCCA, I0 d T_C/(k + d)?
options: It doubles, since d doubles
It is unchanged, because d cancels out of the ratio
It rises by one-third (0.20/0.30 versus 0.10/0.20)
It rises by 50%, because the denominator also grows
explanation: d/(k + d) goes from 0.10/0.20 = 0.5 to 0.20/0.30 = 0.667, a rise of one-third. A faster write-off brings tax savings forward, but the total undiscounted shield is the same, so the PV does not double.

stem: In the salvage term of PVCCA, S_N is the asset's UCC at the time of sale.
options: True
False
explanation: False. S_N is the sale price (salvage value). The lost stream is the CCA the firm would have claimed on that amount of the pool; UCC does not appear in the formula.

stem: The salvage term in PVCCA is discounted by (1 + k) raised to the power _____.
options: d
N, the year of sale
explanation: The value at year N of the lost shield is brought back to today with (1 + k)^N.

stem: Granger Foods owns a line it has been depreciating for years (UCC today $50,000, d = 20%, T = 30%, k = 10%) and will keep it, so the pool stays open. Which expression gives the PV of its remaining tax shield?
options: 50,000 × 0.20 × 0.30/(0.10 + 0.20), with no first-year factor and no salvage term
explanation: An asset already depreciating has used its first-year adjustment (factor 1), and with no sale there is no lost-tail term. The first two options apply a half-year or AII factor that does not belong; the last uses k − d.

stem: Alder Machining buys a $100,000 mill in a 30% class under the half-year rule and expects to sell it in 5 years for $20,000. The tax rate is 25% and k = 10%. What is the PV of the CCA tax shield?

steps.label: Perpetuity base I0 d T/(k + d)
Salvage term S_N d T/(k + d)/(1 + k)^N

errors.label: Used the AII factor
errors.explain: The question states the half-year rule, so the factor is (1 + 0.5k)/(1 + k).

errors.label: Did not discount the salvage term
errors.explain: The lost-tail term is a value at year 5 and must be discounted 5 years.

errors.label: Ignored the sale
errors.explain: The asset is sold in year 5, so CCA on it stops and its tail must be subtracted.

errors.label: Used UCC in place of the sale price
errors.explain: The salvage term uses the sale price S_N, not the UCC.

explanation: Perpetuity base, adjusted for the half-year rule, less the PV of the CCA stream lost after the sale.

stem: A firm buys $250,000 of equipment in a 20% class and the Accelerated Investment Incentive applies. It will sell the equipment after 6 years for $60,000. The tax rate is 35% and k = 12%. What is the PV of the CCA tax shield?

errors.label: Used the half-year factor
errors.explain: The question states AII, so the factor is (1.5k + 1)/(1 + k).

errors.label: Did not discount the salvage term
errors.explain: Discount the lost tail N = 6 years.

errors.label: Ignored the sale
errors.explain: The sale ends CCA on that amount, so subtract the lost tail.

explanation: Same structure as the half-year case; only the first-year factor changes.

stem: Granger Foods owns a packaging line it has depreciated for several years. The UCC today is $240,000 (CCA class rate 10%). The tax rate is 30%, k = 15%, and the line will not be sold: the pool stays open. What is the PV of the remaining CCA tax shield?

steps.label: Perpetuity PV = UCC × d × T/(k + d)

solution: Already depreciating: first-year factor = 1. Not sold: no salvage term.

errors.label: Used k − d in the denominator
errors.explain: The shield declines at d, so the denominator is k + d.

errors.label: Applied the half-year factor to an old asset
errors.explain: A continuing asset has already used its first-year adjustment; the factor is 1.

errors.label: Left the tax rate out
errors.explain: The shield is CCA × T_C.

explanation: 100% regime with no sale: the plain growing-perpetuity value of the shields.

stem: Marsh Bakery buys equipment for $150,000 and pays $10,000 for delivery and installation (capitalized). The class rate is 20%, the tax rate 40%, k = 10%, and the Accelerated Investment Incentive applies. The equipment will be sold in 5 years for $24,000. What is the PV of the CCA tax shield?

steps.label: Perpetuity base I0 d T/(k + d)

errors.label: Left installation out of the capital cost
errors.explain: Installation is capitalized into I0 and earns CCA.

errors.label: Used UCC at year 5 as the salvage
errors.explain: Use the sale price of $24,000.

errors.label: Did not discount the salvage term
errors.explain: Discount the lost tail 5 years.

errors.label: Ignored the sale
errors.explain: The sale stops CCA on that value.

explanation: Capital cost includes installation; AII factor; subtract the discounted lost tail from the sale.

stem: A $600,000 structure is in a 4% CCA class. The tax rate is 35%, k = 11%, the half-year rule applies and the structure will not be sold (the pool stays open). What is the PV of its CCA tax shield?
explanation: Base = 600,000 × 0.04 × 0.35/0.15 = 56,000; half-year factor = 1.055/1.11 = 0.9505; PVCCA = $53,225. $58,775 uses the AII factor; $56,000 ignores the half-year adjustment; $120,000 uses k − d.

stem: A $180,000 asset in a 30% class qualifies for the Accelerated Investment Incentive. It will be sold after 4 years for $20,000. The tax rate is 40% and k = 12%. What is the PV of its CCA tax shield?
explanation: First term = 180,000 × 0.30 × 0.40/0.42 × 1.18/1.12 = 54,183.67; lost tail = 20,000 × 0.30 × 0.40/0.42/1.12⁴ = 3,631.53; PVCCA = $50,552. $48,469 fails to discount the tail; $48,018 uses the UCC at year 4 instead of the sale price; $54,184 ignores the sale.

stem: Rowan Tools owns an asset with a UCC of $90,000 today (20% class), T = 30% and k = 10%. It will sell the asset in 3 years for $15,000. What is the PV of its remaining CCA tax shield?
explanation: The asset is already depreciating, so the factor is 1: 90,000 × 0.20 × 0.30/0.30 = 18,000 less the lost tail 15,000 × 0.20 × 0.30/0.30 / 1.1³ = 2,253.94 gives $15,746. $18,000 ignores the sale; $16,564 applies the AII factor to an old asset; $15,000 does not discount the tail.

stem: When assets are bought and sold in the same CCA class in the same year, net acquisitions equal:
options: total additions minus the lesser of original cost and sale price of each disposal
total additions plus the proceeds of the disposals, since both are cash flows
total additions minus the UCC of the disposed assets at the date of sale
total additions minus the original cost of the disposals, always
explanation: Seminar 5: Net acquisition = total acquisitions − min(original cost, selling price). The lesser-of rule prevents a sale above cost from reducing the pool by more than cost.

stem: A firm buys a new machine and sells an old one in the same class in the same year. Which rule determines the amount to which the 0.5 or 1.5 first-year multiplier is applied?
options: The stand-alone principle
The net acquisitions rule
The capital gains inclusion rule
The salvage-term rule
explanation: The multiplier applies to net acquisitions (a positive net amount). The sale of the old asset reduces the amount that qualifies.

stem: In a replacement analysis, how do the net acquisition cost and the net salvage differ?
options: Net acquisition arises at the end of the project, while net salvage is a cost today
Net acquisition is an after-tax figure while net salvage is stated before tax
Net acquisition = new cost − old resale today (the I0 in PVCCA); net salvage = new − old salvage at the end (S_N)
They are the same number, but net salvage is measured in a later year
explanation: One is the net outlay on the pool today (I0), the other is the net amount leaving the pool at the end (S_N).

stem: Which of the following is NOT used in the PVCCA of a replacement project?
options: New machine cost minus old machine resale value today
Net salvage at the end of the project
The tax rate on the shield
The old machine's book value as the I0
explanation: I0 in the PVCCA is the net acquisition cost, not the book value of the old machine. The old machine's UCC is irrelevant to the replacement PVCCA.

stem: Why does the PVCCA of a replacement use the net acquisition rather than the full cost of the new machine?
options: Selling the old machine removes its cost from the pool, so the pool grows by the net amount
Because the old machine's CCA continues forever and must be netted out
Because the tax rate applies only to the difference in prices
Because tax law forbids any CCA claim on assets bought as replacements
explanation: Additions less the disposal proceeds is the net amount added to the pool, and that is what earns CCA.

stem: A firm's disposals in a class exceed its additions in the year, so net acquisitions are negative. How is the first-year multiplier (0.5 or 1.5) applied?
options: The multiplier is applied to the negative amount, reducing UCC further
No adjustment: the multiplier is applied only to a positive net acquisition
The multiplier is applied to the larger of additions and disposals
The multiplier is replaced by T_C
explanation: Seminar 5: if net acquisition is greater than zero apply the 1.5 times rule to the amount; if less than zero there is no adjustment.

stem: In a replacement problem, the net salvage value (new salvage minus old salvage) can be negative.
options: True
False
explanation: True. If the old machine would have been worth more at the end than the new one, as in the simple replacement example (0 − 10,000), net salvage is −$10,000.

stem: In a replacement, net salvage is −$10,000 (the old machine would have sold for $10,000 in 5 years; the new machine has no salvage). What does this do to the PVCCA salvage term?
options: The term is dropped because net salvage cannot be negative in a replacement
The term is doubled because there are two machines to account for
The term is subtracted with a negative S_N, so it adds to PVCCA; the −$10,000 is also an outflow
The term is discounted at the real rate instead of the nominal rate
explanation: PVCCA = main term − (S_N d T/(k + d))/(1 + k)^N; with S_N = −10,000 the subtraction becomes an addition. Giving up the old machine's $10,000 resale is also a cash outflow at year 5.

stem: When a firm buys and sells in the same class in the same year, the first-year multiplier applies to the _____ acquisitions.
options: gross
average
total
net
explanation: Net acquisitions = additions − min(original cost, sale price) of the disposals.

stem: Fairview Haulage buys a new truck for $340,000 and, in the same year, sells an old truck from the same CCA class for $95,000. The old truck's original cost was $210,000. What is the net acquisition amount?

errors.label: Used the full cost of the new truck
errors.explain: The pool grows only by the net amount after the sale.

errors.label: Subtracted the old truck's original cost
errors.explain: The offset is the lesser of original cost and selling price: here the price, $95,000.

errors.label: Added the proceeds
errors.explain: Proceeds reduce the amount added to the pool.

explanation: Offset the additions by the lesser of the original cost and the sale price.

stem: Hartwell Metals will buy a new machine for $210,000 and sell its old machine (same class, original cost $120,000) today for $70,000. In 4 years the new machine would be worth $25,000 and the old machine $9,000. The class rate is 30%, T = 40%, k = 12%, and the half-year rule applies to net acquisitions. What is the PV of the CCA tax shield?
solution: Net acquisition = 210,000 − 70,000 = 140,000 (the sale price is below the original cost)

errors.label: Used the full cost of the new machine
errors.explain: I0 is the net acquisition cost, not the gross price.

errors.label: Used the new machine's salvage only
errors.explain: The old machine's lost salvage nets against the new machine's: S_N = 16,000.

errors.label: Did not discount the salvage term
errors.explain: The lost-tail term must be discounted 4 years.

explanation: Replace I0 by the net acquisition cost and S_N by the net salvage in the PVCCA formula.

stem: A firm replaces an old machine with a new one costing $180,000. The old machine, whose original cost was $120,000, sells today for $75,000; kept, it would sell for $12,000 in 5 years. The new machine would have no salvage value. The class rate is 20%, T = 40%, k = 10% and the Accelerated Investment Incentive applies to net acquisitions. What is the PV of the CCA tax shield?

errors.label: Used +12,000 as the net salvage
errors.explain: New minus old is 0 − 12,000 = −12,000; subtracting a negative term adds to PVCCA.

errors.label: Ignored the net salvage
errors.explain: The net salvage of −12,000 still changes the shield.

errors.label: Used the full cost of the new machine
errors.explain: I0 is the net acquisition cost of $105,000.

explanation: Net acquisition cost is I0 and net salvage (new minus old, here negative) is S_N; subtracting a negative salvage term adds to the PV.

stem: A firm buys new equipment for $400,000 and, in the same year, sells old equipment from the same class for $62,000. The old equipment originally cost $50,000. What is the net acquisition amount?
explanation: The offset is the lesser of original cost ($50,000) and selling price ($62,000): net acquisition = 400,000 − 50,000 = $350,000. $338,000 uses the selling price although it exceeds cost; $400,000 ignores the sale; $450,000 adds instead of subtracting.

stem: In a replacement analysis the new machine can be sold for $30,000 at the end of the project; if kept, the old machine would be sold then for $12,000. What net salvage value goes into the PVCCA?
explanation: Net salvage = new − old = 30,000 − 12,000 = $18,000. $42,000 adds the two; $12,000 uses only the old machine's value; $30,000 ignores the old machine's lost resale.

stem: A project has sales of $500,000, cash costs of $300,000 and CCA of $50,000. The tax rate is 30%. What is the operating cash flow?
options: None of the above
explanation: OCF = (500,000 − 300,000)(0.70) + 0.30(50,000) = 140,000 + 15,000 = $155,000, which is not listed. $105,000 is net income (CCA not added back); $140,000 omits the CCA tax shield; $190,000 adds the whole CCA instead of T × CCA; $200,000 is S − C before any tax.
